sections.heading: Introduction: Dance as the Living Pulse of Botswana
content: In Tswana culture, traditional dance is far more than mere entertainment—it is the living pulse of the community, a physical expression of identity, history, spirituality, and social cohesion. Botswana's traditional dances serve as a national pride and identity. What makes Tswana dance unique is the styles used to depict various events and moods.

Clapping of hands, leg rattles, whistles and the melodies of songs in different Tswana tribal languages make up special percussions that reveal joy, pain, games and rituals like healing, praying for rain and thanksgiving ceremony after harvest. Each dance is a story told through movement—a celebration of life's milestones, a connection to ancestors, and a bridge between generations.

The dances of Botswana are rooted in the Setswana cultural ethos, combining expressive footwork, live traditional music, call-and-response vocal elements and elaborate patterned sequences that reflect celebratory and ceremonial themes. At their heart, they express the philosophy of botho—humanity and community—through every stomp, clap, and ululation.

sections.heading: Part One: Borankana (Phathisi) – The Dance of the Bakwena

children.heading: Origins and History
content: Borankana (also known as Phathisi) refers to a traditional music and dance genre practiced by the Bakwena tribe in the Kweneng District of Botswana, particularly in the village of Molepolole. Borankana is strongly connected to the culture of Botswana.

According to historical accounts, Borankana performances are estimated to have been initiated between 1914 and 1916. In its early days, it was performed during tribal activities only, and it is believed that only men and boys danced while women sang, clapped hands and ululated.

children.heading: The Origin of the Name
content: The name Phathisi originated from the costume worn during the performance—specifically, the tying of pants on the lower part with a peg, referred to as go phathisa in Setswana. The origin story is deeply connected to the experience of Bakwena men who worked in South African mines:

In the past, men who used to work in mines mostly used bicycles as mode of transport. These men would tie the lowest part of their trousers with a peg when cycling to keep them from being trapped by the bicycle chain and tearing them or end up falling the rider.

For a man to own a bicycle in those days, he had to be wealthy enough to purchase one. The trouser had to be tied hard to avoid toppling of the rider or the trouser being hooked by the chain. The same process of trouser pegging was used when performing Borankana.

children.heading: The Ritual Significance
content: Initially, Phathisi was a ritual dance meant to thank Badimo (ancestors) for good harvests. It was one of the Bakwena's tribal symbols. The dance has since spread throughout the country and even found its way beyond Botswana's borders to places like South Africa.

children.heading: Performance Structure
content: The performance set-up for Phathisi comprises:

items: Men and boys dancing and blowing whistles to enhance the rhythm
The choir (both male and female) wear matlhoa (leg rattles) around the ankles to produce a rattling sound
Dancers wear diphathisi on their shin and beat them with the palms of their hands to produce a 'bomb-like' sound

children.heading: The Connection to Gumboot Dance
content: Cultural observers have drawn similarities between Phathisi and the gumboot dance which traces its roots in South Africa. Gumboot dancing was born in the gold mines of South Africa at the height of the migrant labour system. It has been suggested that gumboot dance may have evolved after Bakwena young men working in the South African mines performed the Phathisi to while away time and entertain fellow miners.

children.heading: The Annual Dithubaruba Festival
content: In efforts to ensure continuity for the Bakwena culture, Phathisi is the main dance performed at the annual Dithubaruba Dance Festival. This festival brings together Bakwena from around the world, especially those from South Africa and Namibia. The festival is meant to strengthen the sense of belonging and pride in the Bakwena people while promoting their culture through music and dance.

children.heading: Performance Attire
content: The attire for Phathisi has evolved over time:

rows: Pants tied down on the lower part with a peg; shorts known as motseto or mongato; diphathisi made from old goat or sheep skin
Skirts made from animal skin referred to as phaeyana, and dressed the top to cover the breasts

sections.heading: Part Two: Setapa – The Dance of the Bangwaketse

children.heading: Origins and History
content: Setapa is a traditional music dance which originates from the Bangwaketse tribe of Kanye village and surrounding areas in Botswana. Setapa traditional dance was started by the Bangwaketse in the past and is therefore regarded as the dance for the tribe.

The word Setapa is derived from the Tswana phrase Go tapa-tapa, which means 'to step into the ground continuously'. This etymology perfectly captures the essence of the dance—a rhythmic, repetitive stomping into the earth.

children.heading: The Meaning of the Dance
content: Setapa is a celebratory style of dance and music characterised by rhythmic stomping, joyful singing, the sporadic sounds of whistles and horns, and garments fashioned from animal skin. The style was originally performed to entertain guests at weddings and other large gatherings.
Setapa is also a dance that celebrates the harvest season, letlhafula, and is characterised by intricate tapping footwork and expressions of joy.

children.heading: Performance Structure
content: Setapa involves a group of people stamping into the ground with their feet to the song played or sung by the choir or the group. Setapa troupes involve an equal mix of both men and women dressed up with the skin of animals.

The dancers wear brown shells in their feet which give out a perfect sound as they dance. The males usually carry whistles and heifer horns to produce sound from the stream of air as they blow into them.

children.heading: The Three Types of Setapa
content: Setapa exists in three different types:

rows: Performed to produce the sound of a galloping horse on the ground
Performed while the lower part of the trouser is tied with a peg or using short pants made of animal skin (tshega). This influence was adopted from the Bakwena tribe dance
Performed by dragging feet on the ground. Go goga maoto means 'to drag feet'

children.heading: Setapa in the Bangwaketse Region
content: The Mmakgodumo culture festival is held annually with the aim of reviving all cultural activities that seem to be slowly fading away in the Ngwaketse region. The festival features poko (poetry), setapa saga Ngwaketse (traditional dance), polka (lobeko style), dikhwaere, dikgafela, and traditional games.

sections.heading: Part Three: Tsutsube – The Dance of Many Interpretations

children.heading: A Dance of Healing and Transformation
content: Tsutsube is a traditional dance that has deep roots in healing practices. Among the Naro communities of Ghanzi District, Tsutsube is recognised as a healing dance. Research has explored the contemporary transformations of healing dances among these communities.
The term tsutsube is widely recognised in Botswana, where it is used as a category for traditional dances. The dance has evolved over time and has been adapted by various cultural groups.

children.heading: Male-Only Performances
content: One of the distinctive features of Tsutsube is that some performances are for males only. A notable Tsutsube song called Nqboku Xlhaie tells the story of a group of young men who have fallen in love with one girl whom they have to compete for. Another song called Khoba is a different version of the Tsutsube dance.

children.heading: Documentation and Preservation
content: The Xere community has undertaken efforts to document their indigenous knowledge, traditional dance commonly known as Tsutsube, traditional songs, and medicinal healing products from natural resources. Through these workshops, the residents realised that they could trade and generate income through their unique traditional dance skills.

Dance groups have expressed interest in adding Tsutsube to their repertoire, alongside other dances such as Wosana, Ndazula, and Mukomoto. Despite the seeming complexity of Tsutsube dance moves, they expressed confidence that they would not have much difficulty in grasping them.

children.heading: Mokomoto
content: Mokomoto is another traditional dance performed in Botswana. It is frequently performed alongside Borankana, Setapa, Phathisi, and Tsutsube by cultural troupes such as the Mogwana Traditional Dance Group.

children.heading: Ndazula
content: Ndazula is a traditional dance that is part of the cultural repertoire of various groups. It is often mentioned alongside Wosana and Mukomoto as dances that troupes seek to incorporate into their performances.

children.heading: Mogwana
content: The Mogwana Traditional Dance Group is a highly respected traditional dance and cultural performance group from Gaborone, Botswana, recognised for preserving and showcasing the rich heritage of Botswana's indigenous music and movement. The ensemble first formed in 1991 as part of Botswana's Silver Jubilee celebrations.

Mogwana's choreography is rooted in the Setswana cultural ethos, combining expressive footwork, live traditional music, call-and-response vocal elements and elaborate patterned sequences that reflect celebratory and ceremonial themes. The group performs Borankana, Mokomoto, Setapa, Phathisi, Tsutsube and other types of dances.

children.heading: Dikhwaere (Community Singing and Dancing)
content: Dikhwaere are mixed choirs that are common in the south of the country in villages such as Mochudi, Kanye, Moshupa, Molepolole and Tsabaong, as well as in the Bobirwa region. Esteemed community singing groups in Botswana include Rangers Marena, Tsa Malwelwe (known for the song 'Mahala'), Zebras, Maphoi and the Naro Giraffe Dance Group.

sections.heading: Part Five: Dance Attire and Instruments

children.heading: Traditional Dance Costumes
content: Traditional dance attire varies by dance type and region but commonly includes:

rows: Worn by women; made from animal skin
Worn on ankles to produce rhythm
Made from phuduphudu skin; worn by Borankana male performers
Principal aerophone instrument that sets the rhythmic pattern of feet movement

sections.heading: Part Six: The Cultural Significance of Dance

children.heading: Dance as Healing
content: Batswana indigenous dance, when danced regularly—alone, with others, or even imagined—offers a healing and coping mechanism for many indigenous people including the youth and elderly. Studies illustrate how Borankana provides healing and support through Indigenous Imagination Dancing.

children.heading: Dance and Social Functions
content: Tswana dance serves multiple social functions:

rows: Weddings, harvest festivals, and community gatherings

children.heading: Dance and Gender Roles
content: Traditional Tswana dance often follows distinct gender roles:

items: Men typically dance while women sing, clap, and ululate
Women participate as singers and percussionists through hand-clapping
Mixed troupes feature equal numbers of men and women
Some dances are performed exclusively by males

children.heading: Dance and Community Building
content: Traditional dance serves as a critical agent in cultural integration. As one cultural observer noted:

'It became vital in uniting Bakwena communities and had that potential to even unite Batswana with other nations as it had grown across borders. As part of our cultural heritage it is seen as a critical agent in cultural integration.'

sections.heading: Part Seven: The Preservation and Future of Traditional Dance

children.heading: Modern Cultural Troupes
content: Several groups are dedicated to preserving Botswana's traditional dances:

rows: Setswana dance, song and cultural expression

children.heading: The National Folklore Ensemble
content: The national folklore group 'Ngwao Letshwao' (meaning 'Cultural Icon') was founded in 2005 in Gaborone with the aim of safeguarding Botswana's culture and spreading its knowledge internationally. The group has created performances that represent the richness and cultural diversity of Botswana.

children.heading: Cultural Festivals
content: Several festivals celebrate and preserve traditional dance:

items: Dithubaruba Dance Festival – Brings together Bakwena from around the world
Mmakgodumo Culture Festival – Revives cultural activities in the Ngwaketse region
Maitisong Festival – Annual ten-day festival at Gaborone Theatre

children.heading: Challenges and Opportunities
content: While traditional dance faces challenges from urbanisation and changing lifestyles, there are also opportunities:

items: Economic potential – Communities can trade and generate income through traditional dance skills
Cultural tourism – Dance is a key attraction for visitors
Youth engagement – Traditional dance inspires younger generations to value Botswana's artistic traditions
Global platforms – Traditional performance can thrive on international stages

sections.heading: Summary Table: Major Traditional Dances of Botswana

rows: Tied trouser legs, leg rattles, whistles, male dancers with female singers
Ritual thanks to ancestors, entertainment, cultural integration
Stomping feet, shells in feet, whistles and horns
